title: A disabled theatre troupe makes able-bodied people the discriminated minority — not to make you feel pity
dek: Yaoyao flips the whole social order: after a nuclear war most people are modified humans, and the few unmodified able-bodied are the 'original sinners' who have to fight for their rights. This isn't a complaint — it's a power fantasy written for disabled people.
why: Mostly oral testimony, no data or research framework; the value is in specific scenes and how one play grew. People who want methodology and industry judgment can skip it.
who: People in public welfare, theatre and amateur workshops; people in content who want to understand why integration can't rely on goodwill alone; practitioners and volunteers concerned with disability issues.
skip: The rehearsal clip at the start and the submission voice-over at the end can be skipped.

points.h: Disabled women being unable to leave home is a widespread phenomenon
points.body: Yaoyao's earliest work was the documentary Han Ya (寒鸦), about three disabled women's struggles with family education and employment. One of the sisters had not left home in 36 years; when her parents took her out to visit relatives during festivals, her feeling was ‘like walking a little dog or cat’. Later she got her first computer, went online, and found a job as a telephone operator — no degree required, only a sweet voice — and after getting the job she bought herself a wheelchair and left home in it. Another visually impaired mother was only allowed to breastfeed her baby for five minutes before her mother-in-law took the child away, saying ‘you can't see, you can't raise a child’; for years afterward she fought her husband's family for custody. These oral accounts made Yaoyao realise that being unable to leave home was not an isolated case.

points.h: Disabled people's friends are all disabled
points.body: A former colleague of Yaoyao's uses a wheelchair; when moving house she could only ask friends who also use wheelchairs, loading wheelchairs front and back with things and hauling them cart by cart. Yaoyao instinctively asked why she didn't call able-bodied friends who can walk upright to help — it would be done in half a day. The colleague was stunned for a moment and said, I don't know any able-bodied people — she did not have a single able-bodied friend, and even her friends all used wheelchairs. Yaoyao said she didn't know how to continue the conversation, and only realised one thing: if disabled and able-bodied people don't even have a chance to meet, ‘you have no chance for integration at all’. This was the direct starting point for her later finding a theatre teacher and making integrated theatre.

points.h: Writing able-bodied people as the discriminated original sinners
points.body: Leyi Theatre's first play, Reverse Future (逆转未来), directly reverses identities: a nuclear war turns most people into disabled people, who through technological modifications like electronic eyes and cochlear implants become new humans; the remaining few able-bodied people, because of ‘the crime of starting the nuclear war’, become original sinners and are marginalised by society. Yaoyao's logic was that since she herself is a mirror-image person, she might as well flip the whole society too, turning all the rights disabled people now have to fight for into rights able-bodied people have to fight for — she calls this writing a power fantasy for disabled people. The core of the plot: an original-sinner father, to keep his son from suffering again because of an able-bodied body, gets drunk, picks up a chainsaw to cut off his son's legs, but ends up in a pool of blood himself; the son is charged with patricide, and the courtroom scenes bring out discussions about original sinners and modified humans.

points.h: How the unseen and the unheard partner up
points.body: Visually impaired actor Wang Xiaomin was pulled in by deaf actor Li Ning to partner during an audition; his first reaction was confusion: you can't hear, I can't see, how do we act. Li Ning's solution was to put his hand on the back of Wang's hand and trace, tapping once when it was his turn to speak. Director Ma Yan said that abroad there is already a form of blind and deaf people performing on the same stage, where the deaf person's hand rests on the visually impaired person's hand, and the visually impaired person can feel the movements. Wang Xiaomin said he had grown up around deaf people, but at the time felt these were two kinds of people born with communication barriers, ‘absolutely impossible to communicate’, and this barrier was almost insurmountable — after this collaboration he and Li Ning became very good friends. The troupe also had to solve sign language interpretation, real-time subtitle screens, and assigning a volunteer to each visually impaired actor for audio description.

points.h: Visually impaired actors wear earphones on stage to cheat
points.body: Only later in rehearsals did the director discover that the visually impaired actors were actually ‘cheating’: they wore earphones, listened to their lines at several times normal speed, and then spoke them seamlessly on stage; the director had no way to assess it and only wondered how the visually impaired actors got their lines down so fast. Conversely, the director didn't know sign language and could only watch everyone signing while laughing on the side, when in fact the actors might be complaining about him in sign language. Once they got familiar, they all knew each other's little tricks.

points.h: She received the Best Play award in the ICU
points.body: In 2024 Reverse Future was selected for the Nanjing New Theatre Festival initiated by Stan Lai. That year Yaoyao had heart problems and was admitted to the ICU; the troupe nearly fell apart, and it was a friend who stepped in to gather everyone for rehearsals and take them to Nanjing. At the closing buffet, while other groups' tables were empty and everyone was dressed up waiting for the awards, only their table kept going back for more food, thinking ‘how could it possibly be us’. In the end they won Best Play, the highest award of the Nanjing New Theatre Festival, and jury chairman Stan Lai stood up and led the applause. At the same time as the award, the news reached the ICU, and Yaoyao lay in her hospital bed in tears. In October of the same year the play was specially invited to the Wuzhen Theatre Festival, as the first integrated disability play, becoming the only production in the ‘No Such Thing as Impossible’ section.

points.h: After writing this play, she changed her answer and chose not to be born
points.body: The second play, I Choose to Be Born (我选择出生), is set in a world where every country legislates that when a fetus reaches eight months, parents must use brainwaves to inform it of its health condition and family environment, and the fetus itself decides whether to be born. Among five families, there are deaf parents who must truthfully tell their child you will also be deaf when born, a husband who deceives his wife into having a child, a family that favours boys over girls, and the last story is adapted from Yaoyao's own experience. The troupe's actors couldn't get through the script because their life experiences were so similar, only the illnesses differed. Asked if they would still choose to be born given another chance, most in the troupe still said they would choose birth, because they still love this world; but Yaoyao changed her answer: she used to say she would choose birth too, now she might choose not to be born, because disabled people are forced to be born into this society, with no choice.

points.h: Same question, Cai Cong and she give opposite answers
points.body: The programme contrasts the deaf couple in I Choose to Be Born with the real-life Cai Cong: Cai Cong and his wife are both visually impaired, and when his wife was pregnant many people advised them to get tests to see if the child would inherit the visual impairment, but Cai Cong did not want to presume that such a life was not worth starting just because the child might also be visually impaired; they believe they can give the child a loving family. The deaf couple in the play decide to let the child be born. Yaoyao and Cai Cong give very different answers, and debate around this choice has always existed. The question the programme raises is: when a family makes a choice, how much choice do they actually have?

facts.v: At age 1 they said she wouldn't live to 3; at 7 or 8 they said she wouldn't live to 12; at 12 they said she wouldn't live to 18.
